title: Trump Cancels $1 Billion in Spending — Without Asking Congress First
summary:
Imagine you and your friends agree on how to spend your allowance. Then someone else decides to take it back — without asking. That's kind of what just happened in Washington.

On Friday, President Donald Trump announced he is canceling nearly $1 billion in spending that Congress had already approved. He used a rare power called a "pocket rescission" (that's when a president tries to undo money Congress voted for).

Most of the cuts hit Health and Human Services programs that help refugees and kids who came to the U.S. without permission. The White House says the money isn't needed anymore because fewer people are crossing the border illegally.

Other cuts target a program for migrant students, an office that works to reduce racial tension, help for minority business owners, and housing counseling.

But here's the twist: Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican from Maine, is upset. She says Trump didn't warn anyone and calls it "a usurpation of Congress's appropriations powers" — meaning he's taking power that belongs to Congress. The Government Accountability Office says the move is illegal.

Congress is supposed to get 45 days to review cuts. But Trump announced them with only five days left in the budget year — and the House is out of session. So the review can't really happen. Stay tuned. This fight is not over.
why_it_matters: The fight is about who gets to decide how the country's money is spent — and the programs being cut help kids, refugees and families, so the answer could affect people in your community.

background_read: Congress (the part of the U.S. government that makes laws and decides how the country spends its money) has to approve spending before it can happen.
A pocket rescission is a rare tool: the president asks Congress to cancel money it already approved, and Congress is supposed to get 45 days to review the request.
The Government Accountability Office (an office that checks how the government spends money and follows the rules) said this move is illegal.
When the president and Congress strongly disagree about spending, it can even lead to a government shutdown, when many government offices close because there is no money to run them.
